title: Practical remote verification of otherwise inaccessible operating reactors

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a practical way to detect, locate and estimate the operating state of a nuclear reactor from outside its site by measuring reactor antineutrinos. It would provide useful information even when direct access to the reactor is unavailable. Success would require a specified reactor power, stand-off distance, observation time and deployment setting, together with quantified probabilities of false alarms and missed detections.

The enabling observation is that reactor antineutrinos can be measured after travelling hundreds of kilometres. SNO+ has demonstrated a combined signal from distant, known reactors using a large underground detector. The proposed advance goes beyond that result: it would infer the presence, location and operation of a target without being supplied its location or operating history. Measuring a known reactor population, reconstructing an interaction inside a detector and locating an unknown reactor are distinct achievements.

significance.text: Conditional significance: if sufficiently sensitive and reliable, an external antineutrino measurement could supply independent evidence of reactor operation. That evidence could corroborate declarations or inform investigations of suspected undeclared activity when site access is restricted. The technical basis is the demonstrated relationship between distant reactor signals and models incorporating reactor power; practical safeguards performance has not been demonstrated by the supplied evidence.

Further implications are conditional synthesis. Validated instruments could support repeated monitoring or regional searches, potentially reducing dependence on information supplied by reactor operators. Their usefulness would depend on sensitivity, response time, background conditions, deployment access, cost and institutional acceptance. Regional coverage would require an appropriate fixed, mobile or networked architecture and a defensible coverage model. Detecting operating reactors would not reveal every nuclear activity, establish the purpose of a reactor or replace inspections and other safeguards evidence.

missing_breakthrough.text: The target capability is reliable inference from a distant signal under practical deployment conditions. The detector must collect enough information to distinguish a target from backgrounds and contributions from other reactors, then support location and operating-state estimates with calibrated uncertainty. SNO+ illustrates the scale of the measurement challenge: its reported analysis used roughly 320 tonnes of scintillator, substantial exposure and a detector 2 km underground. Its systematic uncertainties were smaller than its statistical uncertainties, showing that limited event statistics mattered for that analysis.

Engineering synthesis: a practical system must balance detector mass, observation time, background suppression, deployment depth or shielding, mobility and cost. The research motivates antineutrinos through their penetrating character and weak interactions, but the supplied review does not directly substantiate every general assertion about shielding or interaction strength. The retained measurement supports the importance of mass, exposure and background modelling; it does not establish a universal design limit.

A central inference barrier is the use of prior information. SNO+ modelled known reactor complexes using reactor-power inputs, including hourly electrical-power information for the three CANDU complexes and monthly thermal-power averages for reactor cores. A monitoring system would have to demonstrate what it can infer when target-specific location and operating-history information is withheld. Routine improvements in detector resolution alone would not establish that capability.

Feasibility remains an open question in this record. A compact, economical instrument might fail to meet demanding power, range and response-time requirements, but no physical impossibility follows from the supplied evidence. Requirements must be specified before that tradeoff can be assessed. Likewise, the available sources do not establish that practical unknown-reactor localization remains unavailable across the entire field as of the review's 2026-11-01 reference date.

current_state.text: In its 2025 paper, “Initial measurement of reactor antineutrino oscillation at SNO+,” the collaboration reported a reactor-antineutrino spectral and oscillation measurement using 2020 data. The analysis used 125.4 days of exposure and approximately 320 tonnes of scintillator in a large detector located 2 km underground in Ontario. This is a demonstrated distant-reactor measurement, with the scope and infrastructure of a neutrino experiment rather than a demonstrated compact safeguards instrument.

The SNO+ reactor model attributes nearly 60% of expected inverse-beta-decay interactions from reactors to three known CANDU complexes at distances of 240, 340 and 350 km. That percentage is a model-based attribution within a combined reactor signal, not a measurement locating an unknown reactor. The analysis used known reactor inputs to fit oscillation parameters. Spatial reconstruction discussed for events inside the detector should not be interpreted as reconstruction of a distant reactor's location.

The supplied review reports that all 11 pages of the SNO+ paper were retained and that the relevant prose was readable, although some mathematical extraction was imperfect. The retained HTML omitted table contents and figure images. The conclusions here rely on the prose-supported experimental description, source model and reported result; they do not imply an independent inspection of those documents or figures.

The research lists a paper titled “Mobile antineutrino detector with liquid scintillator for reactor monitoring,” dated July 31, 2026, and describes it as a Monte Carlo study of a proposed mobile detector called NEREUS. However, the source index retains no article or abstract, and the review could not verify the NEREUS identity, simulation methods or deployment status from source content. The earlier statement that only the abstract was accessible is therefore an account in the research, not a verified access finding. The entry remains relevant as a reported research lead, but it cannot establish either simulated performance or an operational deployment here.

The supplied record contains no bounded freshness-search results. It therefore establishes a dated SNO+ achievement without settling the latest field-wide capability, including whether another system has demonstrated practical unknown-reactor localization. Missing evidence for the mobile-detector description does not show that the description is false, and the incomplete freshness record does not invalidate the SNO+ result.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed validation programme: first specify target reactor powers, stand-off distances, required response times, deployment constraints and economic boundaries. Predefine numerical acceptance thresholds for detection, localization uncertainty, operating-state estimation, false alarms and missed detections. These would be proposed criteria for the intended use, not established standards supplied by the cited literature.
completion_criteria.label: Predefined numerical acceptance thresholds within specified deployment and economic boundaries

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: conduct blinded trials against independently recorded reactor operating histories at several realistic distances and background levels. Include reactor-off periods and no-target cases, and declare all information available to the analysis. Withhold target-specific location and operating-history information so that the trial tests independent inference. This addresses a material difference from SNO+, whose source model incorporated known reactor locations and power information.
completion_criteria.label: Blinded trials demonstrate independent reactor inference across realistic conditions

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: repeat the trials across sites and operating conditions, preferably with independent analysis or replication, and verify that uncertainty intervals and error-rate estimates match observed performance. Report the detector mass, infrastructure, observation time and cost needed to achieve each result. Finite tests would establish demonstrated breadth across those conditions, not universal detection capability. Any regional-surveillance claim would additionally require validation of the coverage model for the chosen fixed, mobile or networked architecture, including its gaps and response times.
completion_criteria.label: Repeated trials validate performance estimates and report full resource costs

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: NUC-12, “Reliable, non-invasive, real-time three-dimensional reactor-core diagnosis,” shares the goal of obtaining reactor information without intrusive access. Its target is detailed internal core diagnosis, whereas NUC-05 concerns external detection, localization and operating-state inference. NUC-13, “A fuel cycle with substantially stronger built-in proliferation resistance,” shares a safeguards motivation but changes fuel-cycle properties; NUC-05 supplies observational evidence about reactor operation. These are complementary and distinct capabilities.

Roster-based synthesis: NUC-02, “Mass-produced fission plants with radically lower delivered cost,” and NUC-10, “Long-lived, low-intervention nuclear power for remote sites,” concern deployment and operation of power systems. They could create settings in which external monitoring is useful, but plant affordability or unattended operation would not demonstrate remote verification. NUC-03, “A scalable closed fuel cycle that consumes most long-lived actinides,” and NUC-09, “Very-high-burnup fuel with robust fission-product retention,” concern fuel use and behaviour; an operating-reactor signal alone would not verify their fuel-cycle outcomes or retention performance.

Roster-based synthesis: NUC-06, “Reactor structural materials that remain reliable under extreme neutron exposure,” NUC-11, “Durable materials and chemistry control for aggressive reactor coolants,” and NUC-08, “Broadly applicable passive shutdown and long-term reactor cooling,” address reactor durability and safety. They may affect how reactors operate, but detecting operation remotely does not establish material integrity, coolant compatibility or cooling performance. Each remains a separate innovation.

Roster-based synthesis: NUC-01, “A self-sustaining, net-electric fusion power plant,” NUC-07, “Net-electric fusion using a low-neutron fuel cycle,” and NUC-04, “High-power nuclear propulsion for routine deep-space missions,” concern energy production or propulsion rather than remote safeguards measurement. The supplied fission-reactor antineutrino evidence does not establish equivalent monitoring capability for fusion systems or space propulsion. Their inclusion in the nuclear roster does not imply a shared detectable signature or that completing one would complete NUC-05.

unresolved_issues: What reactor powers, distances, response times, localization precision, error rates and cost limits define practical success for the intended safeguards use?
Does the listed 2026 APS paper describe NEREUS and Monte Carlo simulations as reported, and what performance or deployment claims does its actual text support?
What relevant demonstrations existed by 2026-11-01? The supplied freshness record does not resolve the field-wide state.
Can a compact or mobile system meet the intended requirements under realistic backgrounds and deployment constraints? No feasibility limit or successful implementation is established here.
Which deployment architecture could provide the desired regional coverage, and what blind spots, observation times and access constraints would remain?

brief.title: Finding and monitoring reactors from outside their sites
possible: Inspectors could detect a nuclear reactor, estimate its location and tell how it is operating without entering its site. They would measure antineutrinos, particles emitted by reactors, without needing the target’s location or operating history in advance.
why: Independent measurements could help inspectors check declarations about reactor operation and investigate suspected undeclared activity when access is restricted.
Repeated monitoring or regional searches could reduce reliance on information supplied by reactor operators.

sources.showed: They measured energy patterns in antineutrinos arriving from distant, known reactors using a large underground detector. Their analysis used known reactor locations and power information.
sources.quote: The SNO+ collaboration reports here its first measurement of reactor antineutrino oscillation, using liquid scintillator.
sources.cited_for: Reactor antineutrinos can be measured after travelling hundreds of kilometres.
sources.not_established: The measurement did not locate an unknown reactor or demonstrate practical monitoring without target-specific information.

sources.who: Authors of the mobile reactor-monitoring detector study
sources.showed: This is described as a computer simulation study of a proposed mobile detector for reactor monitoring.
sources.cited_for: It describes a proposed mobile approach to reactor monitoring.
sources.not_established: A simulation study does not establish performance in an operating deployment.

shown: SNO+ has measured a combined signal from distant, known reactors. The experiment used about 320 tonnes of liquid that emits light when particles interact inside it, housed deep underground. This demonstrates distant detection, but it does not locate an unknown reactor.
missing: A practical detector must distinguish a target reactor’s signal from background noise and signals from other reactors.
Blinded trials must establish location and operating-state estimates without advance knowledge of the target.
Repeated deployments must demonstrate reliable error estimates and the equipment, time and cost required.

milestones.label: Success thresholds and practical limits are defined
milestones.explanation: Numerical thresholds would have to cover detection, location, operating state and errors within specified power, range, response-time, deployment and cost limits. These would define useful performance.

milestones.label: Blinded trials identify reactors under realistic conditions
milestones.explanation: Blinded trials would have to infer reactors’ presence, location and operation across realistic conditions, including absent or stopped reactors. Withholding target details would establish independent inference.

milestones.label: Repeated trials confirm reliability and resource costs
milestones.explanation: Repeated trials across sites would have to confirm uncertainty estimates and error rates, report full resource costs and validate any regional coverage claims. This would establish where performance holds and what it requires.

uncertain: It remains unclear whether a compact or mobile detector can meet useful requirements under realistic background conditions.
The reactor sizes, distances, response times and costs that would count as practical success remain to be defined.
Regional monitoring would depend on detector placement, access and observation time, with coverage gaps still to be established.

page.title: Remote reactor detection and localization with antineutrinos
page.definition: An outside-site detector system uses antineutrinos—weakly interacting particles emitted by radioactive fission products—to detect and locate a reactor and distinguish its operating and shutdown states without receiving its coordinates or operating history.

goal.need: The NNSA-commissioned Nu Tools assessment associates cross-border monitoring with detectors of hundreds of kilotonnes, compared with tens of tonnes at shorter range, even before backgrounds. Antineutrinos could provide an independent observable of reactor operation when site access is restricted. The assessment found that detector mass, observation time and backgrounds obstruct non-cooperative deployment.

completion.title: An outside-site experiment detects, locates and monitors a reactor with coordinates and history withheld.
completion.criterion: A peer-reviewed, blinded experiment uses antineutrinos measured outside a reactor site to detect the reactor, localize it to a region smaller than the predeclared search area and containing its surveyed position, and distinguish independently logged operating and shutdown periods. Analysts receive neither target coordinates nor operating history until their inferences are fixed. Thermal power, standoff, exposure, detector mass and depth, localization uncertainty, and false-alarm and missed-detection performance are quantified for the tested deployment.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; no external integrated acceptance test identified.
completion.basis: Searches for IAEA and NNSA acceptance criteria, and checks of Nu Tools, WATCHMAN, SNIF and NUDAR, found component targets and simulated localization, but no integrated blinded test or agreed power, range, time, error-rate, cost or localization limits. This fallback requires an experimental demonstration of the three inferences under stated conditions; it does not establish a numerical definition of practical performance.

milestones.title: Reactor-correlated positron–neutron coincidences establish antineutrino detection.
milestones.criterion: Identify inverse beta decay, in which an antineutrino converts a proton into a positron and neutron, using delayed coincidences, reactor-power correlation and background controls. Cowan and colleagues reported confirmation on 20 July 1956: two independent detector triads, 1,371 hours including reactor downtime, and a signal rate of 2.88±0.22 counts/hour under one selection. Halving the target proton density halved the reactor signal.
milestones.set_by: Experimental-confirmation convention exemplified by Cowan and colleagues in Science, 20 July 1956; this is a detection test, not a safeguards acceptance standard.

milestones.title: A detector 25 m from a reactor identifies shutdown within five hours with greater than 99% confidence.
milestones.criterion: Apply SONGS1's sequential probability ratio test to measured antineutrino counts at 25 m standoff and identify reactor shutdown within five hours with greater than 99% confidence. The 2008 analysis demonstrated this benchmark and reported 3% weekly relative-power precision over a 33-week sample. The NEREUS article published on 31 July 2026 instead describes Monte Carlo optimization of a proposed mobile detector; its accessible abstract reports no deployment result.
milestones.set_by: SONGS1 collaboration, published sequential probability ratio test and experimental benchmark in Journal of Applied Physics, 2008; the benchmark concerns a nearby, known reactor.
milestones.threshold_quote: our current prototype detector can monitor changes in reactor status (on versus off) in five hours with greater than 99% confidence

milestones.title: A detector measures a combined reactor-antineutrino spectrum with major sources 240–350 km away.
milestones.criterion: Obtain a peer-reviewed spectral measurement of antineutrinos from distant known reactors. Published on 10 January 2025, SNO+'s measurement used 125.4 live days of 2020 data, 320 tonnes of scintillator and 45 selected coincidence pairs including backgrounds. Its model attributes nearly 60% of expected reactor interactions to complexes at 240, 340 and 350 km, using their known power histories. This establishes distant spectroscopy, not unknown-reactor localization.
milestones.set_by: Peer-reviewed experimental demonstration, exemplified by the SNO+ collaboration's long-baseline spectral measurement; the distances describe its known sources rather than an adopted safeguards threshold.
milestones.threshold_quote: has measured the oscillation of antineutrinos from distant nuclear reactors.

milestones.title: A detector reconstructs reactor-antineutrino direction with 2.9° azimuth and 1.6° zenith uncertainties.
milestones.criterion: Reconstruct the mean incident direction from positron-to-neutron displacement, with combined statistical and systematic uncertainties of 2.9° in azimuth and 1.6° in zenith. PROSPECT-I reported azimuth 39.4° and zenith 97.6°, consistent with HFIR's known direction, using approximately 48,000 signal event pairs over 95.62 reactor-on days between 5 March 2018 and 6 October 2018. Published on 25 February 2025, this is a nearby-source bearing measurement, not a remote position measurement.
milestones.set_by: PROSPECT collaboration, published directionality-analysis protocol and near-field experimental benchmark; these uncertainties are measured performance, not a safeguards requirement.
milestones.threshold_quote: This direction agrees with the known direction from the reactor to the detector.

milestones.title: A water detector distinguishes reactor-on from reactor-off at 3σ using roughly 30 days in each state.
milestones.criterion: Meet WATCHMAN's 2015 detection criterion: 99.7% confidence (3σ) sensitivity to a full-power reactor using no more than roughly 30 days each of reactor-off and reactor-on data. The proposed baseline was a roughly 1,000-tonne gadolinium-doped water target 13 km from the 3,758 MW thermal Perry reactor. Site criteria also required at least 500 m standoff and no more than roughly 10 reactor antineutrino events/day. The cited document is a design study, not a report that this test was achieved.
milestones.set_by: WATCHMAN collaboration, Section II, Site Selection, of its 2015 design paper; the baseline concerns the known Perry reactor.
milestones.threshold_quote: A signal to background ratio sufficient for 99.7% C.L. (3σ) sensitivity to the presence of a reactor operating at full power

milestones.title: An outside-site antineutrino measurement locates a reactor without supplied coordinates.
milestones.criterion: Measured antineutrino data from outside the site localize a reactor without target-coordinate input; operating-history information may be supplied. The inferred region contains the surveyed position and reduces the predeclared search area. No experimental acceptance test was found. Related evidence is simulated: the SNIF preprint's 1,000 peninsula trials used four 138,000-tonne detectors for one year, a 300±50 MW thermal-power prior and 1,500 m water-equivalent depth; the 68% position-error quantile was 55 km.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback: searches of IAEA/NNSA material, WATCHMAN, SNIF and NUDAR found no experimental acceptance criterion for outside-site position reconstruction with target coordinates withheld. SNIF and NUDAR publish modeled localization studies.

not_found: No published integrated acceptance test for blinded outside-site detection, localization and operating-state inference was found.
No experimental report of outside-site reactor localization with target coordinates withheld was located.
The NEREUS publisher page provided its abstract but restricted article text to subscribers.
